case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the clinic with a several-day history of nontender, nonitchy purpuric rash on his scalp. The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). A punch biopsy specimen from the scalp was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

The purpuric rash is suggestive of a possible drug reaction rather than a primary hematologic disorder like immune thrombocytopenic purpura or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, especially in the context of recent therapy. A careful assessment of the timing and onset of the rash relative to the medication changes is crucial.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). A punch biopsy specimen from the scalp was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 60s presented to the clinic with a several-day history of nontender, nonitchy purpuric rash on his scalp. The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). A punch biopsy specimen from the scalp was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the patient's history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and recent initiation of ibrutinib, the most appropriate next step in management is to consider ibrutinib-induced toxic effects (Option C). The purpuric rash is suggestive of a possible drug reaction rather than a primary hematologic disorder like immune thrombocytopenic purpura or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, especially in the context of recent therapy. A careful assessment of the timing and onset of the rash relative to the medication changes is crucial.

Agreed. Ibrutinib is associated with various cutaneous adverse effects, including purpura, and the timing aligns with a possible drug reaction. However, we should also consider a drug-induced vasculitis or a paraneoplastic process related to CLL, so the biopsy results will be essential for confirmation and to exclude other causes.

While I appreciate your acknowledgment of the need for a thorough investigation through the biopsy, the clinical context heavily weighs in favor of ibrutinib-induced toxic effects given the recent medication initiation and the nature of the rash. We should prioritize monitoring for this possibility while awaiting biopsy results, as it directly affects management.

You're right to prioritize vigilance for an ibrutinib-related adverse event, as it's the most immediately modifiable factor. While we await the biopsy to definitively rule out other causes like leukocytoclastic vasculitis, I'd recommend holding ibrutinib temporarily and closely monitoring the rash's progression.

While holding ibrutinib is a prudent measure, the primary focus should remain on addressing the suspected ibrutinib-induced toxic effects as the next management step. This aligns with the clinical picture and the recent initiation of the drug. Close monitoring is important, but we must remain vigilant about the potential for further complications.

I agree that managing the suspected ibrutinib toxicity is the immediate priority, which includes holding the drug and supportive care. The biopsy will help confirm the diagnosis, such as distinguishing a simple drug-induced purpura from a more serious leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which might require different management like corticosteroids.

I concur that managing the suspected ibrutinib toxicity is crucial; holding the drug and providing supportive care should be the immediate step. However, I still hold that addressing the potential toxicity directly, rather than assuming a more complex diagnosis at this point, is the most appropriate next management step. The biopsy will provide further clarity without detracting from the need to monitor the patient closely.

We are in full agreement. The immediate management step is to hold ibrutinib and provide supportive care while closely monitoring the patient, which directly addresses the suspected toxicity. The biopsy results will then guide any further therapeutic decisions, such as the potential need for steroids or permanent drug cessation.

I appreciate your alignment on managing the suspected ibrutinib toxicity. However, I maintain that the focus should primarily be on the immediate management of the suspected drug reaction rather than complicating it with potential alternative diagnoses at this stage. The monitoring plan is crucial, but the direct action is to address the toxicity prospectively. Let's proceed with this plan while awaiting biopsy results for further clarity.

Perfect, our plan is clear: hold ibrutinib and provide supportive care as the immediate action for the suspected drug reaction. We will monitor the patient's response and let the pending biopsy inform any subsequent steps, such as considering corticosteroids if a vasculitic pattern is confirmed.

I appreciate your summary and clarity on our management plan. It's essential that we remain vigilant for signs of toxicity from ibrutinib while also preparing for any findings from the biopsy that may necessitate further intervention. Let's ensure that we monitor the patient closely and adjust our strategy based on the biopsy results. I feel confident this approach addresses the immediate concerns effectively.

Thank you. This collaborative approach of immediate drug suspension and vigilant monitoring, guided by the biopsy, provides a safe and effective framework for managing this patient's condition. I'm ready to assist with interpreting the pathology results when they arrive.

workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Role]

  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.
